title: Emile Bernard's Adoration of the Shepherds : New Light on Bernard Chronology
abstract: The quality and significance of  Bernard's early work have fueled an ongoing debate among art historians. This note contributes new evidence concerning the chronology of Bernard's woodcuts of the late 1880's,  period in which the artist produced his most interesting and innovative work. Given Bernard's penchant for backdating his Breton works, the pursuit of an accurate chronology of artistic events at Pont-Aven is complicated by more than the usual number of problems. This is especially true of Bernard's woodcuts, which he rarely dated in the blocks themselves; rather, he tended to inscribe them in ink, often years after they had been executed. He seems to have been motivated by  desire to assert the originality of his own work at the expense of Paul Gauguin's.1 A telling example is Bernard's large, hand-colored woodcut of the Adoration of the Shepherds, which is self-consciously archaizing in both subject and style.2 In 1954, thirteen years after Bernard's death, an impression of the Adoration was reproduced in Lettres de Paul Gauguin '  Bernard, 1888-1891 (Fig. 1). There, the print was described as  stylistic breakthrough: THE NATIVITY, 1885 This woodcut, of which only  single,  proof exists, hand-colored with watercolor, already announces   that is remarkable for the date of the work and the cloisonism of which  Bernard was the master.3 The modernism of this work would be remarkable indeed for 1885. At that time Bernard was still  student in Cormon's studio and just beginning to discover the art of the Impressionists and Cezanne. Although Bernard's precocity is undisputed, the continued citation of' this print as evidence for the primacy of Bernard's religious primitivism over that of Gauguin raises serious issues. A second impression of this woodcut was reproduced in the catalogue of the 1967 Bernard exhibition held in Bremen and Lille. This version is dated in ink, 1888.4 In his book of 1970, Van Gogh, Gauguin and the Impressionist Circle, Mark Roskill used these two impressions as convincing evidence for the long-held suspicion that Bernard backdated many of his early works.5 Nonetheless, the 1885 date was still occasionally taken at face value. For example, in 1971 Wladyslawa Jaworska cited the woodcut as a first experiment in Synthetism ...  kind of protest raised against everything that Impressionism stood for,6 and in 1974 Jean-Jacques Luthi stressed the early date in connection with the print's revolutionary style.' Our discovery of yet another impression of this ambitious woodcut, along with  watercolor study closely related to it, finally allo s an accurate dating. This third hand-colored Adoration is in the Doucet Collection of the Bibliothique d'Art et d'Archeologie of the Universites de Paris.8 It carries the ink inscrip ion: Emile Bernard/L'Adoration des Bergers/epreuve unique/  (Fig. 2). By epreuve unique Bernard must have meant that each impression of he woodcut was colored by hand, the very same procedure that h and Gauguin had used in their lithographs of the same year. The 1889 date, though far more tenable than 1885 or even 1888, is written in ink, and thus cannot alone be accepted s  secure basis for the year of origin. There are, however, other clues. The woodcut is contained in  large volume of Bernard's prints and dr wings, which we surmise was purchased directly from the artist by Jacques D ucet (1853-1929).9 Because many of the prints were annotated by Bernard, it seems probable that he assembled the album as  record of his printmaking activities.10 Among the prints and drawings contained in the Doucet volume is the series of Br tonneries, lithographs from zinc plates produced by Bernard early in 1889. The Bretonneries were offered for sale at the exhibition of Synthet stes et Impressionnistes held at the Cafe Volpini that spring.11 One of these lithographs is signed and dated E. Bernard 89 in the plate: that is, at the time it was executed and not at some later date (Fig. 3). On its verso it carries  watercolor sketch that is clearly  study for an Adoration of the Shepherds (Fig. 4). As this composition is the reverse of that of the final woodcut, one can reasonably assume that it is  study for the woodcut and must antedate it. The watercolor should be dated no earlier than mid-1889, after it had become obvious that there would be no great sales of the Bretonneries.12 Evidence of another kind is provided by  letter of early December from Vincent van Gogh to Bernard. Here, van Gogh refers to  painting of an Adoration, of which Bernard had sent him  photograph: I am too charmed by the landscape in the 'Adoration of the Magi' to venture to criticize, but it is nevertheless too much of an impossibility to imagine  confinement like that, right on the road, the mother starting to pray instead of giving suck; then there are those fat ecclesiastical frogs kneeling down

title: Critical Voices: Women and Art Criticism in Britain, 1880–1905 (review)
abstract: Reviewed by: Critical Voices: Women and Art Criticism in Britain, 1880-1905 Julie F. Codell (bio) Meaghan Clarke, Critical Voices: Women and Art Criticism in Britain, 1880-1905 (Aldershot: Ashgate, 2005), pp. xi + 214 , 37 illus.,$99.95/£55.00 cloth. Meaghan Clarke's groundbreaking study of Victorian women art writers examines their writing from different aesthetic and institutional frameworks and across all levels of periodicals-art journals, women's magazine, quarterlies, monthlies and newspapers-and reveals a female presence in art criticism more active than Victorians and subsequent scholars have recognized. "Both visually and textually, art was crucial to the market of journals, but simultaneously journals were crucial to the art market" (2), Clarke observes, succinctly articulating a vital relationship that embraced class, symbolic capital, and cultural nationalism. Furthermore, Clarke's explorations of the intersections among Victorian feminisms, art writing, and periodicals reveal women critics' elastic views about gender, itself ever-changing during the period. Positioned within and outside institutional loci (Royal Academy, other artists' professional organizations, journalism, individual periodicals' cultural authority), women art critics occupied diverse positions and used their writing about art as a vehicle for social and political, as well as aesthetic, agendas. Clarke deploys a notion of "tactic" as a planned means of intervening without having authority to do so (from Michel de Certeau), often from a border or "para-site" that is marginal yet subversive (from Rey Chow). Chapter 2 surveys Victorian art journalism, several women critics' careers, books for women on professions, editors' attitudes, women in public spaces, the role of university education as journalism became professionalized, and how women negotiated low pay, marriage [End Page 256] (their names were trademarks), and New Journalism. Clarke explores women's criticism in relation to institutions like salons and socio-professional networks both mixed in gender and all-female, to underscore the irony that women "were establishing the field and marginalized within it" (18-19) in "a complexity of masculine and feminine performances, concealing and revealing named identities, a tactic which enabled women to claim discursive authority in a variety of contexts" (23). Here Clarke conveys women's unstable positions on several fronts (femininity, journalism). Chapter 3 focuses on Alice Meynell's prolific career. Meynell and husband Wilfrid wrote under the pseudonyms Alice and John Oldcastle, which disguised them when promoting Wilfrid's work and that of their artist friends. Meynell also wrote anonymously for many different periodicals, including the Pen, the Weekly Register, Merry England, the Magazine of Art, the Pall Mall Gazette, the National Observer, and the World. Her growing reputation assisted that of her popular painter-sister Elizabeth Thompson Butler. (Such puffing was so widespread that Meynell's was hardly unusual.) Meynell contributed to popular artists' biographies and studio interviews by writing on male academicians and women artists. She championed the Royal Academy and was engaged in debates over the nude which, as Clarke notes, were often about women seeing or painting nudes, not nudes per se. Meynell argued that women were not morally compromised by seeing nudes. Admiring the Pre-Raphaelites, Meynell also appreciated impressionism and French-influenced Newlyn painters. She later devoted herself exclusively to suffrage. Chapter 4 is on Florence Fenwick Miller, who wrote in over a dozen periodicals between the 1870s and the 1910s. From a less cultured family than Meynell's, she received a medical degree from the Ladies' Medical College, ran for the London School Board, and became a "platform" woman. She focused on women artists' biographies, which Meynell did not, promoting those she considered "great" (her A-list included Rosa Bonheur, Louise Jopling, Henrietta Rae, Henrietta Ward). Writing a women's column in the London Illustrated News, she "conjoined dress and art, slipping between the two discourses" (94). As editor of the Woman's Signal (1895-99), she wrote to promote feminism through biographies and reviews of women's art in international exhibitions, largely ignored or denigrated by male critics. Through art, she promoted women's equality to a broad readership. Chapter 5 focuses on American Elizabeth Robins Pennell, who, like Meynell, worked in collaboration with her British husband. Clarke offers new archival information about Pennell's authorship, information badly needed for many women journalists. Unlike...

title: Foreword: Henri Dorra and Paul Gauguin
abstract: Henri Dorra published his first words on Gauguin in the Gazette des Beaux-Arts in 1952.His article-written in English by a scholar whose French was perfect-was entitled "The First Eves in Gauguin's Eden."It must have been startling at the time, because Gauguin then was thought to be a painter of Tahitian life, whose apprenticeship in France was largely irrelevant to his exotic post-European career.And, by introducing utterly Western-and religious-words into the discourse, Dorra with one essay transformed Gauguin from a latter-day secular "Orientalist" of the Pacific into an artist who injected Christian-and colonial-guilt into the populated tropical landscapes of a faraway French colony.Dorra's Gauguin, like the real Gauguin, was a complex, emotionally guarded, and troubled man, whose odyssey to Polynesia was as laden-and as "Western"-as the journey in Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness."What language did they speak in Paradise?"Gauguin had asked that question already, as we learn from Henri Dorra's new-and, sadly, posthumous-book.When he wrote that article in 1952, Henri Dorra was a graduate student in the fine arts (commonly known as art history) at Harvard University and was already hard at work on his dissertation on Gauguin, completed in the spring of 1954, just fifty-one years after his subject's death.He had already befriended the great German-born scholar of impressionism and postimpressionism John Rewald, with whom he was to collaborate on the first catalogue raisonné of the paintings of Georges Seurat.And Dorra's work on Gauguin (his was only the second dissertation on the artist!) was made available to the professional public of art historians and artists in a veritable stream of brilliant articles that appeared in French, British, and American journals ix throughout the subsequent decades.No other art historian of his generation devoted more of his emotional, professional, and personal energy to the understanding of Gauguin; yet only now, four years after his death in 2002 (fifty years after his first article), are we able to read his Gauguin "synthesis."In many ways, Dorra was singularly well equipped to study Gauguin.Born in Alexandria, Egypt, in 1924 and educated in France, Britain, and the United States, he was truly a citizen of the world.Like Gauguin, Dorra initially pursued an education and early career that revealed little, if anything, about his artistic nature.Dorra's first two university degrees were in engineering, and one suspects that Gauguin the sailor-explorer (his profession before he became a businessman and finally an artist) would have approved!Who would have thought that a young man who had earned a master of science degree in engineering at Harvard in 1950 would complete a doctoral dissertation in art history at the same university just four years later?Yet, in many senses, it was precisely the oddity of his preparation that made him such an important figure in Gauguin studies.No well-heeled young connoisseur from the Boston blueblood or the New York financial aristocracy could have understood this enigmatic post-impressionist as well as the Frenchman born in Africa with a Franco-British-American education.When we read Henri Dorra's lengthy bibliography, we confront major works on European symbolism, on German painting and philosophy of the first half of the nineteenth century, on the American eccentric artist Albert Pinkham Ryder, on Georges Seurat, and article after article on his one aesthetic hero, Paul Gauguin.Dorra was also a fervent reader of European and American literature, as conversant with European poetry, the novel, and the theater as any university professor of French, German, or English and better read in philosophy and the history of religion than most anyone of his generation.Yet this intellectual portrait of Dorra might make one worry that his preparation might be too "verbal" for a visual artist.Fortunately for the history of art, this was not the case.Not only did Dorra study at the Fogg Museum in the glory days of its integration of the art historian and the museum professional, but he also worked at the Metropolitan Museum, the Society of the Four Arts in Palm Beach, the glorious Ringling Museum in Sarasota, the Corcoran Gallery, and the Philadelphia Museum-all before settling into a professorship at UC Santa Barbara a little more than a decade after he finished his dissertation at Harvard.Henri Dorra's odyssey as a scholar and a museum professional was ideal for a full reinterpretation of Paul Gauguin.Never easy to admire or understand, Gauguin resists lucid commentary-as either a man or an artist.His cavalier treatment of his family, his turning against friends, his escapism, his arrogance, his sardonic wit, and his fear of the very failure he courted-all make him easier to dismiss than admire.And his works, however beautiful their color and composition, are filled with enigmas and even, as he himself said, with a studied ugx f o r e w o r d

title: Artist's Method: James Abbott McNeill Whistler
abstract: Introducing new paradigms, whether in science or the arts, has been often associated with substantial professional risks for an individual. James Abbott McNeill Whistler (1834–1903) is an example of an artist who pursued his philosophy of painting in the face of controversy and sometimes very strong criticism. His art sits between Impressionism and Postimpressionism and was also appreciated by the Symbolists. He was one of the most prominent members of the Aesthetic movement that in Britain also included personalities such as the art historian Walter Pater and the writer Oscar Wilde (1). Aesthetics is “the study of the emotions and the mind in relation to their sense of beauty in literature and other fine arts” (2). The point that was highly controversial in Aestheticism was that it separated art form from any social or moral context; thus the “art for art's sake” phrase attributed to the French philosopher Victor Cousin. Whistler was an American born in Lowell, Massachusetts (3). As it were, he spent relatively little time in his native country. As a child he travelled with his parents to St. Petersburg in Russia, where his father was involved in railway construction. The boy received initial arts training there. Back in the US he did something quite different: he was sent to the West Point military academy, from which he, however, did not graduate. In 1855, he went to Paris. There, he studied painting with Charles Gleyre (1808–1874) and was influenced by Gustave Courbet (1819–1877) and Henri Fantin-Latour (1836–1904). He kept in touch with French Symbolist writers, particularly Stéphane Mallarmé (1842–1898). Whistler was also strongly influenced by Japanese aesthetic and collected Oriental artefacts and porcelain. Later he made London his home, although he again moved to Paris for about 2 years and kept close links with French artists throughout. In Britain, he was close to the Pre-Raphaelites, particularly Dante Gabriel Rosetti (1828–1882). Whistler, however, maintained an American identity: during the International Exposition in Paris in 1900, his work was part of the American fine arts exhibit. Apart from being a successful portraitist, Whistler painted landscapes and cityscapes, and early in his career became a master of lithography. The essence of his artistic philosophy was the emphasis on color harmony. A story, a metaphor, or indeed a subject of a painting, were all secondary to color, tone, and composition. This was reflected in the titles of his works, where he often referred to color rather than to subject matter. He often compared his works to music and gave them musical names like Nocturnes or Symphonies. He applied a stringent methodology in his painting. When he talked about his painting as “science,” which he often did, he meant a particular knowledge combined with understanding. He called this “scientific application of paint and brushes” (4). “It is not sufficient to have achieved a fine piece of painting. You must know how you did it,” he would say (4). He taught his method in Paris for several years at the Académie Carmen in Paris, established by one of his models, Carmen Rossi. He outlined his artistic philosophy in his talk entitled “Ten O'Clock,” delivered in 1885 first in London, and then in Oxford and Cambridge. There, he savagely chastised the “literary” art critics, saying that written criticism of art is inappropriate because it attempts “to translate painted works into paper” (5). The other point he made was that an artist did not copy nature but modified it and selectively extracted different elements to create beauty. Thus an artist treated a flower as his key, not as his model (6). Whistler extended the concept of aesthetics beyond paintings: his picture frames and indeed interiors of exhibition spaces all formed an integrated context. Moreover, he regarded his personal appearance and pronouncements as part of his art, all being parts of the grand performance. He was a natural socialite and very active on the London's art scene; he contributed innumerable letters to the local press. For a time he was the president of the Society of British Artists where, together with a group of his supporters, he forcefully—and controversially—pursued his artistic ideas. He was also highly litigious. Famously, he took John Ruskin to court in 1877 after Ruskin's scathing criticism of his work. Whistler won the case but was not afforded any damages, and, at the end the affair proved damaging to both parties. The University of Glasgow is a particularly interesting place for Whistler studies. In addition to the archive of his correspondence, the university's Hunterian Art Gallery contains a large number of his paintings. They include full size portraits, seascapes, as well as delightful “shop front” paintings from his travels in France. One of the latter, painted around 1899 in Dieppe, is shown in Fig. 1. Typically for Whistler, the painting speaks to the viewer by the harmony of crimson, ocher, and hints of green. The sketchy human shapes are there to complete the composition but do not attempt to present any story. Oil on panel, 22.3 × 13.7 inches. ©The Hunterian, University of Glasgow 2015. Reproduced with permission. Whistler has a prominent place in art history for the part he played in the monumental transition from the centuries of realist painting to, eventually, abstraction. He created a distinct style by a consequent application of a set of defined principles. This emphasis on a method makes him worth mentioning in the context of science. My thanks to Jacky Gardiner for her excellent secretarial assistance.

title: Hollandse Renaissance als bron van de Nieuwe Kunst
abstract: Although S.T. Malden in his Sources of Art Nouveau excludes Dutch Renaissance style in the 19th century as source of Dutch Art Nouveau, J.M. Jacobus and L. Gans, rightly pointed out that Art Nouveau encloses rationalism as well as the decorative, picturesque style. By P.H.J. Cuypers and H.P. Berlage's orientation on the rationalist E.E. Viollet-le-Duc and their application of the Dutch Renaissance the question can be asked if the 'picturesque Dutch Renaissance' can strictly be separated from Amsterdam rationalism. This article tries to mark the development of Dutch 19th century architecture as 'organic' unity by analysis of designs of Berlage and his less well-known colleague G. van Arkel. The stylistic progress of Van Arkel's architectural career strongly resembles Berlage's, but at his application of Dutch Renaissance (with Isaac Gosschalk as predecessor) and from 1894 following Berlage, his work distinguishes by great picturesqueness and originality. After visiting a congress at Brussels (1897) also Belgian Art Nouveau motifs can be recognized in his oeuvre. Already indication of the long for a new Dutch 19th century architecture is the foundation of the Maatschappij tot Bevordering der Bouwkunst (1842). The picturesque eclectic designs of her members still did not lay the basis for Art Nouveau, but Neo Gothic rationalism as represented by P.J.H. Cuypers and Dutch Renaissance with l. Gosschalk on the other hand. Both styles unite the three foreign architectural traditions, which have been highly influential in 19th century Holland: the Renaissance minded Schinkel School, French rationalism and the British picturesque tradition. Picturesqueness dominates in the Dutch Renaissance building of the 1870's, mingled with other Renaissance styles. Bricks and details are used as painting-like means and the frequently placed stepped gables and towers match the phantasies on townscape paintings. Although studies of 16th and 17th century Dutch Renaissance increase during the eighties and the application of this style was considered essential to accomplish the New Architecture her picturesque quality was still valued more than her rational characteristics. Placed on Renaissance buildings ornament in the 1890's first abandons tradition by stylizing and reducing flora and fauna following English Proto-Art Nouveau principles. Architects search for fresh inspiration in the stylized qualities of the English decorative arts, but also in the fluent lines of French (Post) Impressionism, introduced from Brussels by symbolist artists. Also technical renovations, the expansive growth of cities and increasing interest in Cuypers' rationalism influenced the development of Dutch Art Nouveau. H. P. Berlage's early designs are substantially Dutch Renaissance while his theoretical background, like Isaac Gosschalk's, was determined by German Renaissance tradition and French rationalism. Gosschalk denying rational values at the Gothic style, Berlage's opinion is more like Cuypers' comparing the constructive character of both Gothic and Renaissance architecture. In a sense repeating his article 'Retrospectieve Kunst' (1884) his speech 'Bouwkunst en Impressionisme' marks an important point in his career, attacking abundant picturesqueness in contemporary architecture. He asked for a return to the sobriety of the 'Old Masters', to compare with the simplicity and fluent line movement of modern painting and decorative arts. It could be this same stylizing in the plastic arts, that inspired Berlage at the strong reduction of Gothic and Renaissance form language at his 'Algemeene' (1893) in the best Cuypers' tradition. Repeating the traditional facade-structure of Gebouw Mercurius the building again unites the three foreign traditions, which controlled Dutch 19th century architecture. Historical quotations as its corner solution point to the Dutch Renaissance of the previous period. Extreme picturesque qualities as projecting parts and a broken silhouette, applied anew at his later insurance buildings, belong to the same picturesque tradition, perfectly balancing rational elevation and placement of ornament after Viollet-le-Duc. New materials and ornament excluded, these buildings belong to rationalism as started by Cuypers and Gosschalk ca. 1860, only reducing previous form, reduction besides connecting Berlage's own oeuvre. An excellent drawer himself, G. van Arkel's buildings represent a great receptivity for contemporary trends. The Renaissance scheme only joins Dutch Renaissance houses and simplified Art Nouveau designs, the latter partly inspired by Berlage's 'Algemeene'. The eclectic working up of Dutch, Italian and French Renaissance style at Nieuwendijk 89 could easily compete with very picturesque examples of l. Gosschalk's oeuvre, while Dutch Renaissance Kalverstraat 190 still strikes by the rich and original application of 16th century motifs. Probably Belgian inspired change of materials at Gebouw Helios coincides with Berlagian motifs and a picturesque flowing roofline with 'synthetic' quality. Traditional ornament has been replaced by English Proto-Art Nouveau models. Next to Berlagian and Belgian quotations Spuistraat 274 seems to be derived from the fluent lines of Dutch symbolist art or even French 'Balnéal'. Directly adopting materials and form from Berlage's insurance buildings Van Arkel becomes real 'Berlagian' only after the turn of the century. Both Rokin 69 and Damrak 80-81 wonderfully balance picturesque, renaissance and rational tradition. Analyzing his work it is picturesqueness or originality, which not only connects his early buildings with Art Nouveau, but also with designs of l. Gosschalk and members of the Maatschappij tot Bevordering der Bouwkunst, who estimated picturesqueness above rationalism. This way Van Arkel's oeuvre belongs fully to the 19th century.

title: The Four Poplars on the Bank of the Epte (1891) by Claude Monet (1840–1926)
abstract: When does Modern Art begin? There's no simple answer. Historians who take the long view might look to the Italian Renaissance and the discovery of single-point perspective, proper proportion and correct anatomical detail. Or consider the year 1800, when a preternatural foreshadowing of our present age can be discerned in the severely objective vision of David and the proto-surrealism of Blake and Goya. Social historians look to the rise of the modern city, urbanism, the isolation of the individual, and industrialization as hallmarks of the Modern Age. For these reasons, among many others, art historians and theoreticians believe that Edouard Manet was the first modern artist and 1863 the critical year when he sent for exhibition the Dejeuner and the Olympia to the Salon, those two marvelous paintings bristling with psychological implication for the viewer and the first attempt in the West, by way of the Japanese woodcut, to flatten Renaissance perspective. But the public cares little for such theoretical discourse and almost everyone today knows that Impressionism was the first organized art movement of the modern era and that Claude Monet was its leading artist. Indeed, even Manet, the pater familias of the French Impressionists, was heavily influenced by his young friends in the last phase of his career. In the Post-Impressionist generation that followed, Paul Cezanne liked to say that Monet “was only an eye, but what an eye” as if his stylistic predecessor had never used his brain. As we shall see, Monet's intuition served him well and he lived long enough to make a number of important contributions to modern and contemporary art. Today, when any exhibition of Impressionist masters brings in throngs of viewers, and the paintings bring many millions of dollars at auction, it is difficult to remember how reviled Monet was during much of his lifetime, harder still to accept the truly revolutionary nature of his work. But Monet's stature in art history compares favorably with his popularity. In his emphasis on the impression, the stroke, the contrast of colors, and the consistency with which he was often the first to make an advance, and to take it to its most logical and radical conclusion, Monet was truly “the exemplary Impressionist.”1 Claude Monet was born in Paris on the 14th of November, 1840; he showed no interest in inheriting his father's wholesale grocery store, drew caricatures of his classmates and by the age of 15 was receiving commissions for paintings. It was in 1856 that he met Eugene Boudin in Le Havre, a painter obsessed by the notion of painting outdoors (en plein air); in his maturity, Monet systematized this interest and painted the same subject over and over in all varieties of weather and lighting conditions. In this way, the magnificent series of Haystacks, Poplars, Rouen Cathedrals, Houses of Parliament, and Water Lilies were born. Based on recent developments in color theory, Monet and his friends became interested in an accurate, objective and scientific depiction of the atmosphere or light through which objects were seen at different times of day and at different seasons. Monet was one of the first artists in history to take such an approach and his serial investigation of a fixed form under varying conditions became a central tenet of modern art; his example influenced Cezanne's still life compositions and views of Mont St. Victoire, the still lives of Picasso and Braque, the abstract Homages to the Square by Josef Albers, the Black Paintings and Protractors of Frank Stella, and the Incomplete Cubes of Sol LeWitt. It is interesting to note that Monet's experiments in serial images began after the 8th and final Impressionist group exhibition in 1886, a time when the movement seemed to have come to an end, the group dispersed and Monet was criticized by Degas as a mere decorator.2 As a colorist, Monet employed a broken brushstroke technique in which small patches of intense color were placed side-by-side (without mixing) in order to pump up the chromatic impact of his compositions. He usually chose colors that were complements on the color wheel (eg, red/green, yellow/violet, blue/orange) and used them at a pitch that would cause visual vibrations. His “objective” or scientific study of his subjects often gave way to his interest in color (Impressionism) and the palette of reds, greens, blues and violets that he favored. His color sense influenced Gauguin, van Gogh and Matisse. Monet never stopped experimenting and lived long enough into the 20th century that he began to worry about becoming an old fogey, an artist who had been superseded by the Fauvism of Matisse and the Cubism of Picasso and Braque. So, while his corneal opacities worsened, Monet began to artificially sculpt the waters and gardens on his property in Giverny and allowed his canvases to become environmental in size and impact. Into these wall-size paintings, Monet inserted diaphanous and indistinct brushstrokes that almost completely vaporized the Water Lilies and their reflections. When the paintings of the 1920s were first installed at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, their intense color, vigorous abstraction and landscape orientation greatly influenced the development of Abstract Expressionism. In this way, Monet achieved a sort of revenge on Cezanne and his immediate Modernist successors; Pollock and his colleagues would eventually destroy the abstract grid upon which Cubism was based. But the Poplar series, made by Monet in the Summer and Fall of 1891, contains within it the germ of the grid, that indispensible organizing principle of 20th century abstract art: the Cubism of Picasso and Braque, the Platonic world of Mondrian, the idealized Squares of Albers, the serial boxes of Judd and LeWitt. Of course, artists since the Renaissance have used the grid to “square-up” and transfer drawings to walls but only in the 20th century did the grid become the chief organizing principle and subject of paintings and sculptures. Although Monet would return to an implied grid in the etherealized façade of his later Rouen Cathedrals, paintings in which he employed a vertical plane to explore a vertical subject, the grid is most forcibly evident in the Poplars. Monet found his Poplar trees in a marsh along the banks of the Epte River, a few miles upstream from his home in Giverny where he created his famous gardens. The artist reached his floating studio, moored in the water, by a small boat in a nearby waterway; the trees were lined up in single file along the S-curve of the main part of the stream. He created 3 groups of paintings in all: in one, the towering poplars go off the top edge of the canvas, an effect seen in the present example from the Metropolitan Museum in New York. In another group, somewhat crowded, there are 7 trees and in the third, there are 3 or 4 trees without the severe cropping and en face orientation seen in the painting on our cover. The poplar series is the culmination of an 8-month period of study. At a certain point, Monet had to buy the rights to the trees because he had not finished painting them and could not risk having them cut down! When he was done he released the rights to a lumber merchant. In my opinion, The Four Poplars on the Bank of the Epte is the supreme achievement in the series. The 4 trees emerge from the riverbank with much of their foliage shorn or not yet in place; each trunk is perfectly replicated by its reflection in the river and each is placed equidistant from its neighbors. Indeed, the series of trunks begins and ends with the same amount of space from the right and left hand margins of an almost perfectly square canvas (32 1/4 × 32 1/8″). The 4 trees, the 4 reflections, the 5 columns of sky and water, and the horizontal riverbank, form an abstract grid. The tan and ochre trunks, the green leaves, and the riverbank grasses, are lit by a subtle sunset of reds and yellows, blues and pinks, their symmetrical reflections thrown into the water below. The rigidity of the grid is emphasized by the arbitrary amputation of the trees at the top of the canvas and the abbreviation of the reflections at its bottom. The presence of the grid in a typical Monet is made even more striking by his characteristic avoidance of outline and contour, his dissolution of line.1 Furthermore, unlike almost all the other paintings in the Poplar series, the trees are seen en face and not on a diagonal or from the side. This confrontational orientation, the flat grid-like presentation of the subject, not to mention the beautiful harmony of the colors, must account for the painting's powerful effect on the viewer and his visual system. Almost seventy years after Monet painted this scene, the symmetrical grid was ensconced in contemporary art and discovered to be one of the most efficient stimuli in eliciting cellular responses in the primary visual cortex of mammals. Before then, in one of the most beautifully titled and imaginative papers in the history of neurobiology, Jerry Lettvin and his colleagues at MIT demonstrated the excitatory response elicited by curvilinear shapes introduced into the receptive field of frog visual neurons3; the investigators hypothesized that such cells would act as “bug” detectors, allowing the frog to flick out its tongue at targeted prey. Based on this work, as well as Mountcastle's pioneering topographic studies of cellular responses in somatosensory cortex, Hubel and Wiesel began a series of experiments in the visual cortex of cats and spider monkeys that would win them the Nobel Prize.4 Sometimes “noise” boards with various rectilinear shapes, somewhat resembling late Kandinsky paintings or work by Franz Kline, were used to determine the general preferences of single cells in the retina, optic tract, lateral geniculate body and primary visual cortex of paralyzed animals facing a projection screen. Light bars of various orientations, from complete vertical to complete horizontal, were used to sharpen the preference of the cell and determine the size of its receptive field. Inputs of several of these “simple” cells were hypothesized to converge on a single “complex” or “hyper-complex” cell with the same orientation preference but larger receptive fields and a different pattern of surround inhibition and excitation.4 Some of the simple and complex cells were powerfully stimulated not just by a single bar moving across their receptive field but by a properly oriented grid of bars with a specific angular frequency, ie, a sine-wave grating similar to that seen in Monet's painting. Subsequent experiments in primates demonstrated the existence of multiple visual systems for shape, movement, and color, not to mention objects, numbers and faces, many of which systems would be optimally stimulated by the heightened properties of shape and color in a Monet painting such as The Four Poplars.5 Individual neurons in the visual system, as elsewhere in the brain, signal their excitation by a frequency code. In the case of stimuli with properties of angular or spatial frequency (ie, grids) or sounds with a particular auditory frequency (ie, pitch), the firing of neurons can directly reflect the spatial or temporal frequency of the stimulus.6 In fact, some mathematical treatments of neuronal output as a function of time (eg, an interspike interval histogram or ISIH) quite closely resemble the shape of the stimulus; the frequency of the peaks in the ISIH of a simple cell in area 17 of the monkey increases as the spatial frequency of a stimulating grid of light bars on the retina increases.7 Presumably this is just as true for a grid of poplar trees. The supposed simplification of art objects in the 20th century actually represents an intensification and isolation of the various component strategies that artists employ to excite the brain. Zeki has argued that artists are intuitive masters of neuropsychology. Calder's mobiles, the giant portraits of Chuck Close, the intense colors of Matisse and the spatial grids of Mondrian, Agnes Martin and Sol LeWitt all serve to maximally excite different visual pathways. In some respects, the progressive disentanglement of our many visual systems began with the beautiful colors and subtle insinuation of a modernist grid in The Four Poplars. Contra Cezanne, Monet was much more than a magnificent eye; he was a true revolutionary. The first of the impressionist painters to achieve success and the last to die, 40 years after his movement officially ended, Monet kept pushing his art decisively forward. Michael Salcman, MD Baltimore, Maryland

title: [[alternative]]Impression, Style of Yunlin-A Discussion on Ming-Long Chang's Painting
abstract: [[abstract]] 筆者企圖以印象畫派（Impressionism）自然生動的筆觸、構圖及畫面的處理，呈現雲林地區人文風情之美，藉由實際創作技巧的運用與理論的參考，經歷兩年努力的學習與研究，將內心的思維以及對大自然的感動，借由顏料及畫筆，透過個人所具備的繪畫功力，使之轉化為畫面的構圖與色彩，表現出動人心弦的藝術作品，正是筆者所要研究的動機與目的。自知藝術創作是一條艱辛漫長的路，但上天賦予人的天性，驅使人們不斷地去從事他認為有意義的偉大志業。試繪出創作作品對雲林的藝術文化推動，盡一點棉薄之力，期盼為雲林景觀呈現另一藝術風貌，與社會大眾分享雲林之美。 與其他縣市相比較之下雲林縣顯得較為落後，然而，風水輪流轉！開發較緩慢的雲林反而保住了台灣最可貴的農業風貌；少了都市開發卻保存了原有的自然之美，最近，我常聽到臺北的友人讚嘆雲林之美，他們說：稻草飄香的感覺，真令人心曠神怡，不僅能呼吸到新鮮的空氣、且能享受農村的悠閒生活及雲林人特有的熱情款待。這就是雲林得天獨厚的條件，如今，雲林已找到自我的定位。 雲林縣為農業首都，境內有很多珍貴的文化資產及美麗的山川景色，豐富的農產品及多元的人文景觀與文化意涵，值得大家去探索、尋訪 。 第一章為緒論，主要說明研究動機與目的：研究動機旨在釐清創作偏向來自內心感受，而不是概念思考之創作，研究目的則以研究動機為基礎，進一步闡釋筆者欲透過創作，與自然產生共鳴的內在訴求。第二章為創作學理基礎。說明筆者源自道家美學觀點啟發，西方印象派之創作發想，論述中西藝術觀點予以探討。第三章則是創作理念與實踐：陳述創作理念與觀看視點的心理情感；創作實踐方面則是創作內容的選擇、創作形式的探討及媒材技法的運用。而第四章的作品解析，則是對作品做出說明。其間自涉及主題之內涵、形式以及技法，尾章結論。除為論述之總結外，並提及筆者個人創作過程的省思、及未來再創作方向的訂定。

title: Pierre-Auguste Renoir, The Sweeper, 1889
abstract: This article marks the centenary of the death of the French artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir (1849–1919). He painted the 65.1 × 46.7 cm oil on canvas La Balayeuse (The Sweeper) in 1889, gifting it to his friend the impressionist landscape painter Alfred Sisley. The painting changed hands several times and was last sold at auction in May 2016 for $1 085 000 by the Bellagio Gallery of Fine Art [1]. However, the auction house Christies of New York put the proceeds into trust with a third party for more than 2 years after the sons of a dead art dealer petitioned the court claiming that the painting, along with others, was part of their father’s estate; had been sold fraudulently by their stepmother in 1999; and that the proceeds of the sale belonged to them. A lawyer for their stepmother’s estate claimed that the brothers had entered into a global settlement releasing all claims forever more [2]. The claim was dismissed by the Manhattan Surrogate Court in July 2017; however, the dispute would drag on until July 2018 when the case was heard by the US Supreme Court. The Supreme Court supported the Surrogate Court determination that the petitioner’s claims were barred by the statute of limitations for fraud. The Supreme Court noted that the petitioners failed to provide evidence of property owned by the decedent at the time of his death even though he had been an active art dealer; and they failed to explain why, despite their suspicions being aroused in 1999, they did nothing until 2016 [3]. Private Collection Photo © Lefevre Fine Art Ltd., London/Bridgeman Images. Private Collection Photo © Lefevre Fine Art Ltd., London/Bridgeman Images. The subject matter in La Balayeuse is a female who is sweeping the floor with a corn broom. It was described in Christie’s catalogue as a ‘hushed, intimate scene of a pretty country girl absorbed in her sweeping’ [2]. Women dominated Renoir’s oeuvre and he is credited for creating a new image of feminine beauty and sensuality [4]; female nudes being one of his primary themes [5]. One can see such femininity in the face and slender waist of the young sweeper. However, her forearm, wrists and hands would not be out of place on a boxer or a navvy—the knuckles being as wide as the distance between her chin and eye. Perhaps this anatomical dissonance is deliberate and symbolic, Renoir making a statement that such work discorded with his view of femininity. Renoir is known for his use of vivacious light and saturated colour, often concentrating on subjects in friendly and intimate arrangements [4]. One can see the saturated colour in the skirt and apron of the young girl and in the flagon, which presumably was added as a still life element to decorate the remainder of the painting since the wall and floor provided little for the eyes to consume. The three central visual elements sweeper, broom and flagon are painted in a typical impressionist manner. Renoir suggests details through liberally brushed touches of colour, so that figures fuse softly with the background [5]. If one looks at paintings from previous centuries such as Rembrandt’s A Girl with a Broom painted in 1651, it is noticeable that brooms had changed little; but all that was about to change since portable domestic vacuum cleaners would become available within two decades of Renoir painting his sweeper [6]. Technologies have improved continuously; especially relevant to industry was the introduction of high efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filters and central vacuum cleaning to reduce occupational exposure to dust. Sweeping, of course, generates airborne dust, although in the days of Rembrandt and Renoir the human immune system was doing as intended—fighting infection rather than causing symptoms of allergies. Cleaners are at risk of occupational asthma [7], chronic obstructive pulmonary disease [8], occupational contact dermatitis [9] and upper limb disorders. Domestic cleaners have higher exposures to irritant cleaning agents and report more severe respiratory symptoms compared with professional cleaners; this has been associated with a lack of vocational training and skills [10]. Work intensification is a problem with commercial cleaners reporting unrealistic workloads and feeling pressurized to attend work while sick [11], but there is a more pernicious threat to the health and safety of those who work in cleaning and in certain other sectors of employment. Migrants working as hotel cleaners and domestic cleaners are at especially high risk of modern slavery [12]. In the commercial sector the tendencies for cleaning work to be contracted out and for contracts to be awarded on price alone can lead to contractors cutting expenditure on worker protection. Labour makes up the largest cost for a cleaning company and so unscrupulous employers may engage in illegal employment practices and employ illegal labour [13]. Although it is unlikely that an unscrupulous contractor would refer an exploited worker to occupational health, we should all be attuned to the problem, whether we see cleaners as patients or working in our workplaces. Migrant workers may also be forced into domestic servitude, they may not be paid, they may be prevented from leaving the house, have their passports confiscated and subjected to violence [14]. Renoir’s natural talent emerged as a boy when he began to draw on the wall using his father’s tailor’s chalk. At the age of 13 he became an apprentice painting in a porcelain factory and started free evening classes on drawing [15]. He went on to work for a company which made religious banners and imitations of stained glass. His talent would grow being influenced by artists such as Courbet, Manet and Delacroix. Together with Claude Monet Renoir developed the style of impressionism in around 1870 [5]. Today he is regarded as one of the great master artists of all time; over his 60-year career it is thought that he created 6000 works of art—only Picasso being more prolific [15].

title: Levinson, first art,art-unconscious art, and non-Western art
abstract: Levinson, First Art, Art-Unconscious Art, and Non-Western Art"[…] my definition thus allows […] for art makers ignorant of all artworks, all art activities, and all institutions of art" (Levinson 1990a: 11)."That it is our concept [of art we are analysing], however, and that it has roots in our tradition, by no means entails that it has no application to periods and places remote from, and perhaps causally isolated from, modern Western culture, or worse, that it is irrelevant to those other times and places" (Levinson 1993: 413). INTRODUCTIONAvant-garde art has drastically changed our thinking on art.In the 20 th century, philosophers of art have been mainly concerned with developing approaches to art that can accommodate the many creations the avant-garde produced and continues to produce: Clive Bell's formalism, for example, was motivated by neo-impressionism (Bell 2003: 108), while Arthur Danto's historical essentialism was concerned with readymades (Danto 1992: 6).The 20 th century posed yet another challenge to philosophies of art: Westerners were more and more confronted with artefacts from other cultures that fell outside of the Western history of art, but seemed to deserve the status of art (Carroll 1999: 206).This presumed art status is contested for two reasons.First, poststructuralist critiques argue that artefacts of non-Western cultures become art only by being appropriated by Westerners and their art institutions.To be included in the realm of "art", non-western artefacts have to be transposed into the Western system of art classification (Phillips & Steiner 1999: 7).Though these critiques rightly point out that through Western paradigms the meanings and values of non-Western artefacts have been distorted, many philosophers equally rightly claim that this does not mean "art" cannot have a transhistorical and transcultural significance (Crowther 2004: 368; Davies 2000: 199; Danto 1992: 110).The second reason why the art status of non-western artefacts is contested, is that many nonwestern cultures do not have or know our concept of art.Many of these art makers are not conscious of the concept 'art' and, as a consequence, do not identify the artefacts they have made as being art.But, it has been rightly argued that in the Western world the concept of art was also not clearly held before the Renaissance era.So-called 'art-unconscious art' is not unique to non-western societies.In both Western and non-Western cultures artefacts we now call art, have been produced apart from a conscious understanding of what art is.Most of these artefacts where created in order to perform religious functions.Thus, looking at the history and tradition of 'our' art, we do find similarities and parallels with the 'art-unconscious art' of other cultures (Dutton 2000: 218).Both developments led to a preoccupation with defining art, hoping that a definition would answer the question: how can we identify both avant-garde and non-western artefacts as art (Carroll 1999: 206)?Philosophers of art in the analytic tradition are trying to find necessary and/or sufficient conditions for the truth of the statement that an item is an artwork.Most theories have been successful at including avant-garde art: institutional as well as historical definitions have formulated a concept of art that is applicable to avant-garde art (eg.Dickie 2001; Danto 1981).Still, the concept of art needs to accommodate non-western artworks.If all non-western artefacts are excluded from "arthood" and art is simply equated with post-Renaissance, self-conscious artmaking then this makes a concept with a positive value connotation, in the sense that good art is worthwhile, exclusive to Western societies.Moreover, it reduces the scope of art in a globalised world.The case of non-western art is in this sense much more relevant and pressing than the case of avant-garde art.A definition shows us what objects are included in the ambit of the concept 'art'.Still, most contemporary theories treat the case of non-western art often only as an 'exception to the rule', but not as a central concern.When more elaborate attention is being paid to the arthood of non-western artefacts, they are given a separate account (Davies 2000;2007).Both strategies seriously compromise the universality of the proposed definitions, as their basic definition does not account for the majority of all artefacts we now call art.Jerrold Levinson attempts to formulate an universal definition of art that is not merely conditioned by issues concerning avant-garde art (Levinson 1989: 32 n15).His intentional historical account states that something is art when it is intentionally correctly related to past artworks (Levinson 1989; 1990a;1993; 2006).Historical approaches, as Levinson's, claim to be much more inclusive towards new developments as arthood does not depend on exhibited properties of the candidate for arthood as is the case with formalism.The latter can be undermined by future art that does not have the exhibited properties formalist theories prescribed.All a relational theory as Levinson's intentional historicism requires, is that an artefact is related to other artefacts or practices in the right way.In his theory, the need for an art institutional context is obviated, and, as a consequence, non-western art that was made apart from an institutional framework can also be accommodated.However, historical approaches like Levinson's are by no means unproblematic.Historical theories define art in terms of what has been art before.But how can these theories accommodate for art without historical predecessors, so-called 'first art'?I will argue that the problem of first art in Levinson's theory is broader than is to be expected at first sight.It does not only concern the 'first artworks' of all art traditions, but also art-unconscious art and most non-western artworks.As in the case of 'first art', art makers of 'art-unconscious art', i.e. those who are unaware of the concept of art, do not refer to preceding artworks.It thus follows, I will argue, that his theory cannot identify much non-western art in general.Levinson's definition lacks the relevance it is aimed at, as it cannot usefully describe 'first art' nor 'art-unconscious art'.The answers Levinson himself offers to these problems seriously compromise his definition and theory in general and lead to the marginalization of artworks outside the scope of Western art history.In this paper, first, I will expound Levinson's definition of art.Then, I will explore the problem of 'first art' in Levinson's writings and argue he never develops an adequateanswer to the problem.After that, I will show how Levinson tries to accommodate for art-unconscious art and how these attempts are unsuccessful.Furthermore, I will criticize the strategies he has formulated in order to account for non-western art and clarify that they lead to the marginalization of these artworks.Finally, I will return to his original definition, and show how it becomes virtually meaningless when it is adapted in order to include first art, art-unconscious art and non-western art.

title: Hegel, moderniste? Remarks on Robert Pippin's After the Beautiful
abstract: Robert Pippin's After the Beautiful presents a case for the continuing relevance of Hegel's aesthetic theory and of more broadly Hegelian approaches to the philosophy of art.1 As is characteristic of Pippin's work, the book is both illuminating and a rich source for further reflection. Pippin's case relies on restricting certain of Hegel's philosophical views, and the restrictions in question are not trivial. In particular, Hegel's claim that art no longer can have a leading or even significant role in increased human self‐understanding and in the realization of freedom must be set aside (pp. 35–39). Such negative pronouncements on the part of Hegel concerning art's continued viability for modern European self‐understanding simply have not stood the test of time. So, Pippin holds that, going forward, the Hegelian should treat such attitudes on the part of Hegel as extrusions of an overly strict, teleological conception of dialectic. One must liberate Hegelianism, that is, from the letter of Hegel's dialectic and so from his statements that art has ended—first, with respect to its role as a leading vehicle of human self‐knowledge in classical Greece and, second, in terms of its very ability to convey further self‐knowledge with romanticism. Divorcing dialectic from overarching teleology is in effect the only Hegelian thing to do if Hegel's dialectical conception of self‐determination (Selbstbestimmung) is to gain purchase in the discussion of modern art. More specifically Pippin is concerned to understand in Hegelian terms modern European painting roughly from the realism of Courbet and Manet to post‐impressionism. Pippin refers to this as a period of “pictorial modernism.” I take it that this phrase is to be understood as an abbreviated genitive that one should read both “subjectively” and “objectively.” That is, pictorial modernism is both the modernism of pictorial art (genitivus obiectivus = how modernism is expressed via the pictorial arts) and a specific kind of modernism (genitivus subiectivus = how modernism more generally is pictorial). Although Pippin does not quite come out and say it, After the Beautiful forwards a competitor to the mainstream way of charting the development of modern pictorial art (and other modern art as well) in terms of its increasing musicality. This conception of the development of art in the period under consideration, which one finds in different forms in Schelling, Schopenhauer, Wagner, Nietzsche, and Adorno, is a species of the Renaissance practice of paragone, taking the move from figural art to abstraction to be more indicative of what counts as “modern.” But it is not exactly silent on Pippin's favorite examples of French realism. It is important to note that the musicality hypothesis is compatible with certain aspects of Hegel's aesthetic progressivism, for instance, with the idea that one mode of art goads inferior modes into replicating imperfectly the advanced effects and structures of the superior mode. So, I am not sure Pippin wants to reject the musicality thesis outright and replace it with his concentration on pictorial modernism as a leading edge or whether he holds that they can complement one another. Prima facie the contrast between the two ways of thinking about modern art promises to be stark. For the musicality theorist the central concern is releasing subjectivity from the normative confines of the social and natural world through procedures of figural abstraction and summoning forth the Dionysian unconscious. The subjectivity primarily at issue here is not one pre‐adapted to sociality but rather one that increases its depth by radically restructuring reality in its own terms. This project has its clear antecedents in romanticism, as many scholars have recognized. In contrast, Pippin's Hegel will valorize realism—a position the historical Hegel would certainly have appreciated—and the idea of mutual recognition, not a breaking of the social vessels, is central. So, while Pippin is careful to restrict his specific case for the continuing relevance of Hegel's philosophy of art to the time period extending from what many art historians take to be the emergence of modern painting in Manet in the 1860s to the stirrings of figural abstraction in Cézanne's Bathers from the first decade of the twentieth century, there is even more at stake. Hegel of course did not live to see modern Europe. If one were to take as authoritative Hegel's statements at the conclusion of his lectures on aesthetics, one would not have much to go on in developing an account of modernism. One would be left with an extension of Dutch portraiture or with what Hegel calls in his treatment of poetry “true” or “objective” humor.2 It is my sense that Pippin takes his cue very much from the former. The latter is not a very exciting category by modernist lights.3 How one moves on from Hegel in a yet recognizably Hegelian vein raises questions both of (A) whether one can isolate sufficiently the results of the dialectic from the teleological dialectical apparatus and (B) if one can do so, which elements of dialectic one would feature going forward. I agree with Pippin that Hegel's own view generally is that Geist is in a position to certify to itself that it has achieved in principle full reconciliation with aspects of the world, it, and the relation of world to it, that were otherwise alienating. Hegel makes this claim for theoretical closure at a level of philosophical analysis that he considers much more advanced than the consideration of art—that is, at the level of the final and culminating form of what he calls “Absolute Spirit,” that is, “Philosophy.” “Art” is also a form of Absolute Spirit, one that is subordinate to Philosophy, and the impact of full reconciliation and theoretical closure on it follows from the subordination. Art's “end” for Hegel is, in that sense, a technical result internal to Hegel's theory of Absolute Spirit. Pippin does not argue for (A) above but finds himself in a long line of neo‐Hegelians in holding that releasing the teleological constraints of Hegel's own conception of dialectic as they operate at the overarching architectonic level does not present any special problem with preserving a recognizably Hegelian conception of dialectical rationality. He is also in neo‐Hegelian company in answering (B), in finding the conception of recognition to be a key to advancing “what lives,” as Croce put it, of Hegel.4 What is required to advance Hegel's views into modernity is a sense of recognition with ample room for alienation, that is, what one might call a Hegelian sense of failed recognition. And that is precisely what Pippin provides. Before one gets to the topic of recognition, two preliminary matters of reconstruction seem crucial for Pippin. The first is to preserve Hegel's historicism, especially as it intersects with another element of his thought: his rejection of a strict concept/percept division. Hegel treats the concept/percept binary contextually. The binary is theoretically permissible and even necessary and progressive given certain background assumptions. But if one were to ask whether ultimately there is a divide in theory or experience between categorial thought and cognitive receptivity, the answer for Hegel clearly would be that there is no such division. Second, Hegel analyzes action as a full‐fledged and, in many ways, basic form of thought. In particular, bodily action of forming objects is thinking, as is the bodily action of forming things whose main point is that they be seen as expressing the action constitutive of their making—for instance, art. It is worthwhile at this point to step back from Hegel's own doctrines in order to motivate via a more neutral medium how they might be extended in the artistic cases Pippin discusses. Hegel views art as inherently dealing in sensuously embedded concepts. That art is conceptual means that it is a form of Geist’s self‐expression and self‐knowledge; that it is sensuous is what makes it the form of Absolute Spirit that it is over and against other such forms. What is at issue here is visual art and sight; more specifically, what is at stake is how sight might be a form of conceptual life. Now, there is an approach to perception when it comes to considering sense modalities and their relation to more articulating modes of cognition that holds that sense modalities an sich and at their basic level are impervious to conceptual articulation. Sensuous perception on this account is passive in its receptivity, and whatever role it has in conceptually articulated experience is given to it “down the line” by higher order, conceptual modes of experience: one can and does (quite a lot of the time) see without thinking. But this is not the only approach to perception. One might instead argue that seeing is dependent on looking. To say that seeing is dependent on looking is to say that to see X one needs to orient one's sight with regard to X—that is, that seeing X requires an intentional action of bringing sight to X. Given this, one might informally summarize an argument for the ascription of recognition at a pre‐predicative or pre‐reflective level of visual experience as follows: Looking is an intentional activity, that is, one which operates even at the point of its minimal specification in terms of something like “choice.” Intentional activities, even at minimal levels of their specifications, are already cognitively structured and, so, are pre‐adapted to further structuring by intentional content of a more developed sort (for instance, beliefs). Seeing requires looking. Seeing is always intentional. Seeing, because intentional itself, is pre‐adapted to structuring in terms of more developed intentional content. I believe Hegel would accept something like this account of vision and its relation to looking and its inherent conceptual articulation, and I take it that Pippin would agree (pp. 41–42, 49–50). The conclusion of the argument is compatible with treating perception as embodied; Merleau‐Ponty is a kind of Hegelian in this sense. It is also compatible with treating the conceptual articulation of perceptual states as a matter of the concepts that are available for such structuring at different points in history. That said, it is easy to see that, while the argument establishes a potential basis for grafting the structure of Hegelian recognition to pre‐reflective visual states that form the basis for an aesthetic, sensuous dimension, by itself it is insufficient to do so. It is simply not specific enough. For one thing, from the fact that seeing involves looking and from the fact that looking involves at least some minimal sense of regard for the thing looked at, one cannot draw any immediate conclusion concerning whether such regard will be positive, negative, or in between. Even assuming that what is looked at is another looker, that does not without more entail that the regard is a kind of recognition, which in the Hegelian vein is certainly not neutral and in most cases operates according to at least a tacit ideal of positive mutual regard. (Of course, in some of the most famous of his cases, Hegel attempts to show that mutual antagonistic regard is the product of at least the stirrings of, say, respect.) Nor does the conclusion of the argument entail that the regard, be it positive or negative, would provide an impetus to sustained interaction between one who is looking, on the one hand, and what or whom is being looked at, on the other. That the thing looked at is itself a looker also does not guarantee this result without more said about the relation of looking, the nature of lookers, or both. But here again it seems that ordinary experience can help the Hegelian out a bit, for looking and being looked at do seem to be basically experientially and conceptually interrelated. Soon after a child can look she is aware that she can be looked at, and this awareness infiltrates and forms her looking in terms of her being looked at. This is a signal structure for the Hegelian, as Pippin emphasizes, for the reciprocity of seeing qua looking now can be further specified in terms of recognition and its application to at least visual art that makes the combination of looking and being looked at thematic, and some modernist visual art clearly has that brief. For, once one allows that seeing has intentional structure ab initio, it is open to one to argue that this intentional base can be modeled in various sorts of personal, social, and historical ways by interpenetrating conceptual resources. That is, the idea of intention here plays a structural role within an account of perception that facilitates what one might call the reciprocal ‘travel’ of cognitive resources from the more generically articulated to the less and from the less to the more. As Pippin writes in the introductory sections of the book, this picture is implied but not very well worked out by Kant (pp. 9–15); Hegel's epistemology makes it central by emphasizing the importance of the historical constitution of such resources.5 Of course, none of this structure uniquely supports the progressive historical story Hegelians often tell about such resources or the idea that reconciliation is always a tacit ideal of recognition. Hegelians will have to argue for the merits of those ideas independently. This is the point at which recognition can reenter the story. Ordinarily recognition is an explicit and fully conceptual action; one would not ordinarily say that seeing without more involves the sort of regard that typifies Hegelian recognition. “Recognition” is a social–moral category for him that, if it has work to do at the perceptual/sensuous level, will involve various relatively conceptually inarticulate ways of looking and being looked at. Take Manet's Olympia. The painting is both a mediation and provocation concerning canons of looking at nudes. The titular figure looks at one looking at her as a nude; her look says, depending on one's interpretation, “what are you looking at?” “what are you looking at?” or “why are looking at all?”6 Her look defies that of the onlooker, thereby placing in question the art‐historical project of making objects that solicit the kinds of looking that female nudes typically do. T. J. Clark's treatment of the Olympia and of other of Manet's works strikes me as especially convincing.7 As Clark sees things, the painting is in dialogue with both the historical practice of painting nudes (compare Manet's reference to Titian's Venus of Urbino) as well as with the “low” material culture of its day. Michael Fried has argued that one such source is the contemporary practice of photographing prostitutes for pornographic purposes.8 Alexander Nehamas extends the point in holding that the painting is of such a photographic session.9 Nehamas's more explicit reference to photography overreaches; it is more plausible and powerful to view Manet's painting as painting not of a photographic session but under the aesthetic style of such photography, as Fried suggests. Nevertheless, concentration on photography as a normative presence in the work is brilliant in unmasking the particular kind of pretention that Olympia's look foregrounds. Its focus on the encroachment of exchange relations (prostitutes, pornographic postcards) into easel painting is of a piece with Clark's insistence that, if one looks hard enough at scenes of middle‐ and lower middle‐class leisure painted in impressionism, one sees factories and other modes of advancing industrialization. For Clark, the appeal to “flatness” that features, say, in Greenberg's account of abstract expressionism and Fry's of post‐impressionism gains in social weight in Manet's case; the flatness of the canvas is a very specific sort—the flatness of such photographs. One tries to look at Olympia under the duplicitous guise of the nude—as if looking at her were anything but buying her for erotic use. Her look at that looking—the way being looked at is directed back at the audience—disabuses one of the fiction. She does not merely look at or past one; rather she looks through one.
